entries.title: Dion and Theon
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Checked the modern SEP formulation of the whole-limbed Dion and Theon as the remainder excluding the right foot; the apparent survival/coincidence problem; the later report in Philo and the answer attributed to Chrysippus; Philo’s objection; the van Inwagen response; and the article’s brief mention of other material-constitution positions. This status records source traceability for those claims, not a settled ancient interpretation, philosophical truth, consensus, or expert review.
entries.summary: The article now distinguishes the SEP’s modern right-foot formulation from the testimony preserved in Philo, attributes the Dion-survives/Theon-perishes answer to Chrysippus as reported by Philo, and identifies Philo as the critic. The van Inwagen passage has been corrected to track the SEP’s account of the simples constituting part of Dion’s life before the operation and composing Dion afterward. Modern material-constitution positions are labeled as later options rather than readings of Chrysippus. An independent reviewer checked the revised article and dataset; the source location and paraphrase issues it flagged were corrected before status assignment.

sources.title: Material Constitution
sources.author: Ryan Wasserman
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Spring 2026 archive; first published 2009, revised 14 January 2026.
sources.access_level: The relevant portions of the fixed archived entry were read; the whole entry was not audited systematically.
sources.exact_locations_read: §1 presents the Dion and Theon puzzle, identifies Theon as the part of Dion excluding the right foot, and states the apparent problem. §2 explains van Inwagen’s response: the simples initially constitute part of Dion’s life and, after the operation, compose Dion. The entry’s overview and treatment of coincident objects support the carefully limited note that other later material-constitution positions differ.
sources.limitations: Secondary reference, not Chrysippus’s own text. The right-foot setup is attributed to the SEP’s modern presentation, not projected onto Philo’s wording. The brief overview of other views is not an exhaustive survey of solutions to Dion and Theon.

sources.title: On the Eternity of the World
sources.author: Philo of Alexandria; translated by C. D. Yonge
sources.publication: Sections 48–49; English translation hosted by Early Jewish Writings.
sources.source_type: Primary ancient testimony / later report of a Stoic argument
sources.access_level: The English text of the relevant sections was read; the complete work was not read systematically.
sources.exact_locations_read: §48 introduces Chrysippus’s puzzle, states the principle that two specifically qualified individuals cannot jointly occupy the same substance, and poses which person has been spoiled. §49 records Philo’s objection and the explanatory reply attributed to Chrysippus that Dion survives while Theon perishes.
sources.limitations: Philo is a later witness and critic, not Chrysippus. His report is brief and interpretively disputed; no extant Chrysippus text was consulted.

sources.title: Chrysippus’ Puzzle about Identity
sources.author: John Bowin
sources.publication: Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy 24 (2003), 239–251; author-hosted scan reproduction.
sources.access_level: The paper’s opening account and relevant interpretive discussion were read in a full-text scan; the whole article was not audited line by line.
sources.exact_locations_read: Opening, pp. 239–240, quotes Philo’s report and notes that it is notoriously cryptic; the paper discusses Sedley’s reading and Bowin’s alternative interpretation across pp. 239–251. Bibliographic details were cross-checked against the PhilPapers record https://philpapers.org/rec/BOWCPA.
sources.limitations: A secondary interpretation, not a resolution of the ancient passage. The present educational article does not adopt Bowin’s interpretation as settled.

claim_evidence.material_claim: In the SEP formulation, Theon is the part of Dion excluding the right foot; after the foot is removed, Theon’s parts seem unchanged, which creates a survival and coincidence problem if Dion survives too.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1, opening discussion of the Dion and Theon puzzle.
claim_evidence.finding: The source supports this as its modern formulation. The revised article explicitly attributes the right-foot version to the SEP rather than treating it as the exact wording of Philo’s report.
claim_evidence.limitation: The scenario is a later exposition of the ancient testimony; no original text by Chrysippus survives in the consulted sources.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: separated the SEP’s specified right-foot version from the broader ancient report.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Philo reports a Chrysippean answer that Dion survives and Theon perishes because two specifically qualified individuals cannot occupy one substance, then objects that Theon lost no part while Dion lost a foot.
claim_evidence.source_title: On the Eternity of the World; Chrysippus’ Puzzle about Identity
claim_evidence.exact_location: Philo §§48–49: §48 gives the setup and question; §49 gives Philo’s objection and Chrysippus’s explanation. Bowin, opening pp. 239–240, quotes and conventionally cites the report as De aeternitate mundi 48 (SVF ii.397).
claim_evidence.finding: The translated testimony and Bowin’s scholarly reproduction support the attribution and the objection. The article consistently says this is Philo’s later report of Chrysippus, not Chrysippus’s own surviving text.
claim_evidence.limitation: The report is brief and cryptic; the precise force and original dialectical purpose are disputed.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: identified Philo as the transmitter and critic and qualified Chrysippus’s attribution.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Van Inwagen’s response denies that Theon exists as an object before the operation; the relevant simples initially constitute only part of Dion’s life, and after the foot is removed they constitute a life and compose Dion.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2, discussion of van Inwagen’s eliminativist view and its application to Dion and Theon.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP supports this modern response. The article’s paraphrase was corrected to track the distinction between the simples constituting part of Dion’s life before the operation and composing Dion afterward.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is van Inwagen’s modern position as summarized by the SEP, not an ancient solution attributed to Chrysippus.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the paraphrase and cited SEP §2 rather than §1 for this response.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Modern material-constitution views differ over coincident objects, identity, persistence, and which objects exist; they are later options rather than a settled interpretation of Chrysippus.
claim_evidence.exact_location: The entry’s overview of replies and §§2–6 on coincident objects and alternative approaches to material-constitution puzzles.
claim_evidence.finding: The entry documents distinct modern positions. The article describes these only as a brief map of the broader debate and explicitly disclaims a consensus reading of the ancient argument.
claim_evidence.limitation: The source’s main focus is material constitution generally; the article does not claim each view was developed specifically as a direct answer to Dion and Theon.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed the unsupported four-dimensionalist and sortal-specific solution list; retained only a qualified overview tied to material-constitution debates.

entries.title: The Grelling–Nelson Paradox (Heterological Words)
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Checked the standard autological/heterological setup and self-application contradiction; the qualified formal analogy with Russell’s set paradox; Ramsey’s meaning-relation response and the Tarski connection; the paper’s authorship and 1907/1908 publication metadata; and the article-to-dataset reference alignment. This does not establish that any proposed solution is definitive or that the original paper has been fully examined.
entries.summary: The article now states the self-application assumptions needed for the contradiction, distinguishes the semantic paradox from Russell’s set paradox, and limits its historical solution discussion to Ramsey’s meaning-relation approach as summarized by the SEP. The publication line records both the catalogue’s 1907 entry and its 1908 reprint rather than collapsing the discrepancy. The original paper and its publication volumes were not directly inspected. An independent read-only reviewer found no essential factual correction; it verified the definition, structural analogy, Ramsey/Tarski summary, and exact URL order.

claim_evidence.material_claim: A predicate is autological if it applies to itself and heterological if it does not; applying the heterological definition to itself produces a yes/no contradiction under the stated assumptions.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1.1; compare §3.3.2 in Paradoxes and Contemporary Logic for a translated formulation.
claim_evidence.finding: The source supports the standard setup and self-application contradiction. The revised article makes explicit that the result depends on applying the definition to itself and requiring a yes/no classification.
claim_evidence.limitation: The original paper was not read; the article explains the standard reconstruction rather than reproducing the primary argument verbatim.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified the assumptions under which the contradiction follows and kept examples explicitly illustrative.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Grelling–Nelson paradox is structurally analogous to Russell’s set paradox, but concerns semantic predicates rather than sets.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1.4, formal comparison of the paradox’s structure with Russell’s set paradox.
claim_evidence.finding: The source explicitly makes the formal comparison. The article describes it as structural and states that the paradoxes concern different kinds of things.
claim_evidence.limitation: The analogy does not imply that semantic predicates and sets are the same kind of entity or that their solutions are interchangeable.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the analogy and removed broader unsupported claims about type theory and definability.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Ramsey’s response distinguishes the meaning relation used in the definition from the relation needed to express the meaning of the adjective, blocking the unrestricted self-application; the SEP connects this with later Tarski-style semantic hierarchies.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3.3.2, Ramsey’s treatment of Grelling’s paradox and the subsequent note about Tarski.
claim_evidence.finding: The source supports the distinct-meaning-relations explanation and says these ideas foreshadow Tarski. The article presents this as one historically discussed response, not a definitive solution.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article does not claim Ramsey formulated Tarski’s later theory in full or that all versions of the paradox are solved by one move.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced an unsupported list of non-classical and contextual views with the source-supported Ramsey response and an explicit scope limitation.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The source record documents a 1907 publication and a 1908 reprint; the SEP cites 1908, so the article should preserve rather than erase the discrepancy.

entries.title: McTaggart’s Paradox of Time
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Checked the A-series/B-series distinction; the move from change to the A-series; the incompatibility and successive-predication argument; McTaggart’s tensed reply and regress; the article’s reconstruction caveat; the broad A-/B-theory descriptions; the qualified relativity connection; publication metadata; and ordered source alignment. This is not a judgment that McTaggart’s argument succeeds or that one theory of time is correct.
entries.summary: The revised article now summarizes the A/B distinction and McTaggart’s two-stage argument with the primary text’s relevant pages read in a full-text scan reproduction. It avoids saying the A-properties apply simultaneously, explains the successive-predication reply and regress, and marks the three-premise reconstruction as one standard form because the SEP notes reconstruction disputes. Modern A-/B-theory and relativity statements are qualified to match the SEP discussions. An independent reviewer found no essential correction; the primary scan metadata, article references, and dataset URLs align.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The A-series orders times as future, present, and past, while the B-series orders them through earlier/later relations; McTaggart says genuine change requires the A-series because B-series relations do not change.
claim_evidence.source_title: I.—The Unreality of Time; John M. E. McTaggart
claim_evidence.exact_location: McTaggart pp. 458–465; corroborated by SEP McDaniel §3 and SEP Time §4.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text supports the distinction and the change argument; the SEP entries corroborate the standard reconstruction. The article attributes the claims to McTaggart rather than presenting them as established facts.
claim_evidence.limitation: The scan is a reproduction and the reconstruction’s details are discussed by later commentators.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified the sequence of premises and stated that McTaggart argues B-series relations alone are fixed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: McTaggart argues that incompatible past/present/future determinations apply to each event successively, and that the reply using ‘was future, is present, will be past’ presupposes time and generates a regress.
claim_evidence.source_title: I.—The Unreality of Time; John M. E. McTaggart
claim_evidence.exact_location: McTaggart pp. 468–470; SEP McDaniel §3 on the contradiction argument and its contested reconstruction.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text supports the successive-predication and regress summary. The revised article does not say that the three properties apply simultaneously and notes that later A-theorists need not treat McTaggart’s objection as decisive.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a simplified educational summary; it does not establish that the regress is sound or the conclusion follows.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the common simultaneous-predication gloss and explained the tensed reply.

claim_evidence.material_claim: B-theory and A-theory are broad families with multiple positions; presentism and growing block are distinct A-theoretic views, while relativity of simultaneity challenges but does not by itself refute A-theory.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §§5–6, discussion of A-/B-theory, presentism, growing block, and relativity of simultaneity.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP supports the range-of-views framing and treats relativity as a challenge whose implications depend on additional assumptions. The article explicitly avoids treating physics as a decisive verdict on the metaphysical debate.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article does not survey all A- and B-theories or resolve the metaphysical/physical assumptions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the relativity connection and separated presentism from growing block.
